en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai says:

Regarding the explanation of the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa," the Sanskrit term for *stūpa* (or *thūpa*) is translated here as "square mound" (*fāng fén*), and is also called a "spiritual temple" (*líng miào*).
Furthermore, it is said that a *caitya* (支提) is a site where no physical remains are present.
Since this stupa contains the entire body without dispersal, it cannot be termed a *caitya*.

The *Āgama* clarifies the four *caityas* (*cetiya*), meaning that stupas are erected at four locations: the place of birth, the place of attaining enlightenment, the place of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and the place of final nirvana. This present jeweled stupa is the *caitya* of the former Buddha’s entry into nirvana.

The Sūtra states: "The three bodies of the Buddhas are born from this sūtra; it is here that all Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment, it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, and it is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa. Indeed, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the fourfold essential limb of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The Buddhas of the past have already resided here, the Buddhas of the present sit together here, and the Buddhas of the future shall do likewise.
This stupa has emerged to manifest this matter clearly for the fourfold assembly to behold; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jewel Stupa."
In the *Sutra of the Necklaces*, Subhūti asked, "Are the merits of the birth-body, the universal body, and the fragmented body equal?
The Buddha said, "They are not equal.
The physical body speaks of teaching and training; when the three karmas are fully perfected and pure, sentient beings can reach the site of enlightenment."
"The completely pulverized śarīra possesses majestic spiritual power and radiance; by making offerings to it, one obtains merit. For this reason, they are not equal.
He then asked the Tathāgata Śikhin, "If you have preached the Dharma and transformed beings for twelve nayuta kalpas, and your śarīra is likewise so, then these two should be equal."
The Buddha said, "All of this is produced by the supernatural power of Tathāgata Cūḍāmaṇi-rāja.

In that previous sutra, the entire wooden case was shattered and the śarīras emerged solely through the power of the Buddha in his birth-body (*jāti-kāya*). Now, in this sutra, both the complete shattering of the wooden case containing the birth-body śarīras and the emergence of the perfectly round śarīras of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) from within the sutra manifest the vast power of upholding the merit of this scripture. To testify to this matter, [the stupa] surged forth from the earth, and the fourfold assembly all witnessed it; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa."
The Master of the Northern Region said:

"When the Buddha was preaching the sutra for Śāriputra, the jeweled stupa had already appeared to serve as a witness. If the preaching of the sutra were to end, what would there be for it to come and witness?"
"The Sūtra compiler established the sequence by placing [this event] after the three cycles [of preaching]"—such a view based on mere human sentiment is not to be trusted.

Now, according to the *Sālaṃkāra-vatī-sūtra*, it says: "When the Buddha was preaching the *Lotus Sūtra* with innumerable verses, a stupa made of the seven precious jewels emerged from the earth. Within it was a golden throne, and upon the throne was a Buddha named Pao-hsiu-lan-lo (Vairocana), which in the Han language means 'Great Treasure. He praised the Honored One of the Śākya clan, saying:"
"I have come specifically to make offerings; I pray that you will sit upon my golden couch and further preach for me the *Sālaṃkāra-puṇḍarīka*.

Based on this scriptural evidence, it is clear that three cycles [of preaching] were delivered, after which he again requested the teaching on the lifespan. Since the explicit text of the Sage’s own words exists yet is refused to be accepted, how can one rely on such human fabrications?

This stūpa specifically emerged from the earth to testify to what was previously requested and subsequently fulfilled; since the fourfold assembly all witnessed it, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jewel Stūpa.
The masters of the *Dìlùn* school maintain that Prabhūtaratna is the Dharmakāya Buddha;
the *Śāstra* states that Prabhūtaratna manifested as a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to come and testify to this sutra, and this passage is likewise so.

The Master said: "The Dharma-body has neither coming nor departing; the Reward-body is majestic and sublime; the Response-body universally responds to all things. If one were to claim that these [three] are themselves the three Buddhas, one would not have exhausted their essence; they are merely symbolic representations. The Many-Treasures Buddha represents the Dharma-Buddha, Śākyamuni represents the Reward-Buddha, and the manifested bodies represent the Response-Buddha. Although the three Buddhas are three, they are neither identical nor different. One should speak in this way and believe and understand in this way."
These four sections correspond to the four *siddhāntas*, as explained in the "Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa" chapter, and so forth.
The emergence of the stūpa is twofold:
first, it emits a voice to corroborate what preceded; second, it opens the stūpa to initiate what follows.

Regarding "realizing what was previously [taught]": this means realizing that the teachings of the three cycles are all true and real. To speak briefly of what is true and real: it is that which accords with the *dharmatā* (the true mark of reality).
To speak extensively of what is true and real: it is that which transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
To speak of it from the middle way: the "eight negations" are termed true and real.

The stupa emerging from the earth demonstrates non-extinction; sharing a seat and sitting together demonstrates non-arising; entering the stupa demonstrates non-permanence; manifesting the stupa demonstrates non-interruption; the division of the body demonstrates non-identity; the whole body demonstrates non-difference; the many jewels yielding their seats demonstrates non-coming; and Śākyamuni sitting upon half the seat demonstrates non-going. These eight negations are clearly manifest; therefore, this is the reality.
Furthermore, it is proven that the propagation of this "trace" teaching involves profound merit in upholding the sutra and great power in its extensive dissemination;
all of this is true. As for "equal great wisdom," how does it compare to *prajñā*?

The *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 79, states: "Prajñā is the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, just as one enters through a city gate from any of the four directions. One should know that Prajñā is also termed the "Wondrous Dharma," while this sutra terms it "Equal Great Wisdom" (*samatā-mahāprajñā*); by these two texts referring to one another, their intended meaning can be understood.

Regarding "arising after": if one wishes to open a stupa, it is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and clearly entrust them with the profound teachings, so that the sound reaches the lower realms to summon the original disciples and discuss the span of the Buddha’s life. Then, stupas from long ago emerge from the earth, manifesting the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) to reveal how he benefited sentient beings in past ages.
He utters a great sound, manifesting the power of the lion’s majestic leap to reveal the provisional and disclose the ultimate throughout the ten directions.

Possessing great vows, he ensures that whenever future Buddhas preach this sutra, his precious stupa shall arrive at those places to serve as a witness, manifesting the power of great majesty and ferocity to reveal the eternal and indestructible nature of the future.

Furthermore, the stupa appearing in mid-air also verifies that what arose later was present before. Those at the seven stages of expedient means have their storehouse of principle not yet opened and remain obscured by ignorance, like the stupa remaining on the ground.

Upon hearing the three turnings of the wheel, the three gates are opened and reality is revealed; the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are disclosed, and the Dharma-body is manifested, like the stupa surging into the sky—this verifies what was previously present.

Having cultivated and attained the Dharma-body, it has long been manifest and evident, like the stupa in the sky which no one can open; this signifies that the original ground has long been accomplished, yet remains unrecognized by the multitude.
If one reveals their original station and manifests their fundamental nature, attaining complete understanding without doubt, this constitutes the introduction to what follows.

As for the stupa emerging from the earth, it symbolizes the manifestation of the Dharma-body; it is both similar to and different from other sutras. It is similar in that Bodhisattvas manifest the Dharma-body, but it is different in that the Two Vehicles manifest the Dharma-body.

If the stupa is in the air and opens its doors so that one may see the Buddha, this signifies the revelation of the hidden traces and the manifestation of the original source, which is forever distinct from other sutras.
If the stupa comes to bear witness, the preceding matter has already been made manifest; there is no need for doubt.

Regarding the stupa’s arrival after [the Buddha] has risen, it possesses a secret meaning unknown to the multitude; now, to adopt the latter sense and provide this preliminary explanation is likewise without fault.

Regarding the interpretation of "contemplating the mind": when one cultivates contemplation based on the sutras, the realm and wisdom corresponding to the Dharma-body will inevitably meet, just as the stupa appeared to testify to the sutra. Once realm and wisdom have met, the great retribution is fulfilled, as in the case of Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna sitting together upon a single seat. Because the great retribution is fulfilled, the Buddha manifests responses according to the capacities of beings, as if all the emanations had gathered; because they emerge from the stupa of Prabhūtaratna, the three Buddhas become manifest, and because of upholding the sutra, one possesses the three bodies. As the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* states, "The three bodies of the Buddha arise from the Vaipulya [sūtras]," this is precisely that meaning.

Some divide this chapter into eleven subsequent chapters, asserting that from here on the "Body Wheel of Supernatural Powers" (*ṛddhi-kāya-cakra*) reveals the original and the trace; however, they argue that from the "Questions of Maitreya" onwards, it is the "Speech Wheel of Dharma" (*vāk-cakra*) that reveals the original and the trace, and thus it is too early to make such a textual division before the meaning of the original and the trace has been fully manifested.
This chapter consists of prose and verse.
The prose section has three parts:
first, the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna; second, the gathering of the emanated bodies from afar; and third, Śākyamuni’s proclamation of the invitation.
The initial section contains six parts:

first, the manifestation of the stūpa; second, the offerings of the devas; third, the praise of Prabhūtaratna; fourth, the astonishment and doubt of the assembly; fifth, the inquiry of Mahāpratibhāna; and sixth, the Tathāgata’s response.

Regarding the phrase "a stupa made of the seven treasures," this clarifies that the ground of the Dharma-body attains the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven treasures of the noble ones by virtue of its intrinsic nature; "stupa" refers to the realm of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), which is the locus upon which the Dharma-body relies.
"Five hundred yojanas in height" refers to twenty thousand *li*, vertically illustrating the ten thousand practices within the cause and the ten thousand virtues within the fruit.
"Two hundred and fifty yojanas in breadth" refers to ten thousand *li*, horizontally adorned by the ten thousand wholesome deeds.
“Earth” refers to the mind-ground of ignorance (*avidyā-citta-bhūmi*); by having nothing to destroy, one destroys ignorance;
by having nothing to dwell upon, one dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
"Various precious objects" refers to the adornment of manifold concentration and wisdom.
"Railing" refers to the dhāraṇīs.
"Myriad chambers" refers to the chambers of immeasurable compassion, as well as the dwellings of immeasurable emptiness.
"Banners and streamers" are the supreme signs of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Hanging jeweled necklaces" refers to the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*), which adorn the Dharma-body above and clothe sentient beings below.
"Ten billion jeweled bells" refers to the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Fragrance emanating from the four sides" refers to the wind of the Path of the Four Truths blowing forth the fragrance of the four virtues.
"Reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings" means that he has exhausted the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
From "the Heaven of the Thirty-three" downward, the second section concerns the offerings of the various devas; while the literal meaning is clear, it may further be understood in terms of principle.

The thirty minds constitute thirty [stages], the ten stages constitute one, Equal Enlightenment constitutes one, and Sublime Enlightenment constitutes one; together they total thirty-three, all of which equally rely upon the realm of true reality (dharmatā).

Regarding the phrase "Raining down Mandārava Flowers": the initial mind also possesses the merits of the forty-two stages, and the final mind is likewise so; all are flowers of the causes belonging to the forty stages that are directed toward the Dharmakāya.

The passage beginning with "the other devas and nāgas" refers to those at the stages of inner and outer ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who likewise rely on the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to practice the causes directed toward the fruit.

The section beginning with "At that time, from within the jeweled stupa" is the third part: the praise by Prabhūtaratna, which serves as the formal verification that the previous revelation of the provisional to manifest the ultimate was not in vain.
“Equal Great Wisdom” refers to the wisdom of all Buddhas, analogous to the principle of walking with even steps as described previously.
There are two kinds of equality:
first, the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*), which is the Middle Way.
Second, regarding "equality among sentient beings": all sentient beings equally attain the Buddha-wisdom.
"Great" (*mahā*) has the same meaning as previously explained as "lofty and vast.

From the perspective of contemplating the mind: the contemplation of emptiness is equal vertically; the contemplation of the provisional is equal horizontally; and the contemplation of the Middle Way is equal both horizontally and vertically. This simultaneous illumination of both [aspects] in equality is precisely the Great Wisdom of Equality.
"Thus, thus" means: first, it is as the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are; second, it is as their fundamental natures (indriyagotra) are.
"All are true" means that they are called true because they are spoken of in accordance with the characteristics of phenomena.
"Then the fourfold assembly saw... and so forth, marks the fourth section: the astonishment and doubt of the assembly.
This passage contains two parts:
first, the attainment of the joy of Dharma; second, the arising of wonder and doubt.
From the passage "At that time there was a bodhisattva" onwards is the fifth section: Mahāpratibhāna’s inquiry based on doubt.
In view of the intent of the subsequent answer, there should be three questions;
the first question is: "For what cause does this stūpa exist?"
The second question asks: "For what reason does the stūpa emerge from the earth?
The third question asks: "For what reason is this sound emitted?
From the passage beginning with "At that time the Buddha told... is the sixth section, the Buddha’s response.
Regarding these three points:
first, the second question is answered first; because this Buddha has a vow to serve as a witness for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he emerges from the earth.

The section beginning with "When that Buddha attained enlightenment" is a retrospective answer to the first question, explaining that it was by the command of that Buddha that this stupa was constructed.
Next, from "That Buddha, by means of his supernatural power... onwards, the third [section] answers the third [question], producing this sound in order to provide testimony.
The *Śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was unable to preach the Dharma before entering parinirvāṇa; however, the Master’s interpretation is not so.
That Buddha told the bhikṣus—bhikṣus being those who are to be transformed by the teaching—why would he not speak?

It must be that although Many Treasures (Prabhūtaratna) also attained the opening [of the Dharma], he could not manifest the reality; therefore, the *Śāstra* says that he was unable to preach the Dharma.
For this reason, although [the Tathāgata] has entered parinirvāṇa, wherever the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is preached, he immediately rejoices and bears witness to it.
From the passage "By the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, Mahāpratibhāna," onwards is the second section, which clarifies the distant gathering of the emanated bodies.

In this regard, there are seven points: first, the desire to speak and the request to see Prabhūtaratna; second, the gathering of the emanated Buddhas; third, the desire to speak and the request for the assembly; fourth, the emission of light to summon them from afar; fifth, the arrival of all the Buddhas together; sixth, the adornment and purification of the realm; and seventh, the granting of consent to open the stupa.

Regarding the first request, the phrase "relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power" (*buddhānubhāva*) means that in order to open the stūpa, it was necessary to assemble the Buddhas; once the Buddhas were assembled, they conferred their entrustment (*parindanā*); having conferred the entrustment, they summoned those from the lower regions; and when those from the lower regions appeared, the near was opened to reveal the distant. Since this is the origin of such a great matter, is it not indeed the Buddha’s spiritual power that enables the inquiry?
The remaining sections are as in the text.

Regarding the passage beginning with "At that time, the Buddha emitted light from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows," there are four parts; the fourth is the emission of light to summon [beings] from afar.

As for the "purification of the land through three transformations," this is primarily due to *samādhi*. There are three types of *samādhi*: first, the transformation of the Sahā world, which is the *vipaśyanā* (liberation) capable of transforming the defiled into the pure.
Next, he transforms two hundred nayutas; this is mastery over the transformation of superior states.
Finally, he transforms two hundred nayutas; this is being unimpeded regarding all objects in every state.

Furthermore, the first transformation-purity represents the purification and removal of the four abodes; the next transformation-purity represents the purification and removal of the sands of dust; and the final transformation-purity represents the purification and removal of ignorance.
"At that time, the various Buddhas sat upon lion thrones. This is the seventh [section], "Granting Permission to Open the Stūpa," which further consists of five parts:

first, the various Buddhas inquire after one another’s welfare and express their consent; second, Śākyamuni opens the stūpa; third, the fourfold assembly all witness and hear [the same]; fourth, the two Buddhas share a seat and sit together; fifth, the fourfold assembly requests the addition [of the Buddha's presence].
The various Buddhas collectively grant their consent (*chanda*) to open the stūpa, just as the formal procedure for granting consent is performed within the Saṃgha.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* clarifies that several Buddhas grant their consent; the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* likewise states that several Buddhas from the ten directions together expound the *Avataṃsaka*; and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also says that a thousand Buddhas together expound the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

None of these state that they are emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni. According to the present sūtra, they must indeed be emanations; however, because those [other sūtras] employ skillful means (*upāya*), they do not explicitly reveal this during that particular time.
Now, this sutra does not merely consist of a great number of items; it also directly states that all these emanated bodies have come to express their assent (*chanda*).

From the passage "At that time, Śākyamuni saw... onwards is the second section. Opening the stupa is the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*), while seeing the Buddhas is the revelation of the ultimate (*bhūta-artha*). This both serves as a verification of what preceded and prepares for what follows.
"Like removing the bolt and key" means removing the obstacles that hinder the movement of the mechanism.
From "With a great voice" onwards is the second section, in which Śākyamuni calls for volunteers to seek out those who will propagate [the teaching].
It further consists of three parts:
first, the loud proclamation of the recruitment.
From the words "The Tathāgata will not be long" onwards is the second part, clarifying that the time for the entrustment has arrived.
The section beginning with "The Buddha wishes to... constitutes the third part, clarifying that there is a specific recipient for the entrustment. Regarding "having a recipient":
while the Buddha was in the world, he benefited sentient beings according to their capacities; he personally expounded the True Dharma without depending on others.

Now, as the Buddha’s conditions for transformation have reached their limit and his capacity to respond has ended, he wishes to ensure that this Dharma brings benefit without end; therefore, it must be entrusted to others for circulation.
Regarding the phrase "the entrustment has a locus," there are two meanings:
first, the immediate locus of the entrustment, wherein he commissions eighty thousand and twenty thousand bodhisattvas who have long resided here to propagate [the teaching] in this land;

second, the ultimate locus of the entrustment, wherein he commissions the atoms of a thousand worlds beneath his original disciples to ensure its circulation everywhere, and furthermore, to initiate the revelation of his lifespan.
The verses consist of forty-eight lines, praising the three preceding points:
the first three and a half lines praise the parinirvāṇa of Prabhūtaratna;
the second eight and a half lines praise the gathering of the emanated bodies.
The third section consists of thirty-six lines and explains Śākyamuni’s entrustment (*parindanā*).
The first two parts are as the text reads.
From "He addressed the great assembly" onwards is the third part, which further divides into two:
The first eight and a half lines cite three Buddhas to encourage the circulation [of this teaching];
the subsequent twenty-seven and a half lines cite the dharma that is difficult to uphold to encourage its circulation.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, one and a half lines, which recruit and seek out such persons;
second, from "As for that Prabhūtaratna... onwards, there are three lines, which formally cite the three Buddhas to exhort the upholding of the sutra.

Next, from "Those who are able to protect" onwards, the third section consists of four lines; it explains the intent of the exhortation by stating that being able to uphold this sutra is itself making offerings to the three Buddhas and beholding the three Buddhas.

From "O sons of good family" onwards is the second section, consisting of twenty-seven and a half lines, which exhorts the circulation of the Dharma by citing its difficult-to-retain nature. This section is further divided into two parts:
first, twenty lines, which directly cite the exhortation;
second, seven and a half lines, which explain the intent of the exhortation.
Regarding the first [section], there are again three parts:
first, one line, which provides exhortation and admonition;
second, from "The other various sutras" onwards, seventeen lines, which formally raise the difficulty of upholding [this sutra] to encourage its circulation.

The section beginning with "In the future, for the sake of the Buddha-way" constitutes the third part; these two lines explain the meaning of upholding [the Dharma] with difficulty. If one can uphold it, one is upholding the body of the Buddha—how could this intention be easy?

Second, the seven and a half lines beginning with "O sons of good family, I [have... clarify that he can uphold what is difficult to uphold and can accomplish supreme virtues, thereby explaining the intent of the exhortation.
This section further consists of three parts:
first, one and a half lines, which re-enlist those who uphold the sutra;
second, from "This sutra is difficult to uphold" onwards, another one and a half lines, clarifying that the Buddhas rejoice and praise those who can uphold what is difficult to uphold.

Next, from "This is indeed valorous" onwards, the third section consists of four and a half lines, clarifying that being able to uphold what is difficult to uphold constitutes a supreme practice; this supreme practice includes both the self and others.

Regarding "the world of fear" (*bhayabhīru*): in Indic it is called *sa-pai*, which here means "fear"; in Indic it is called *bhadra*, which is simply another name for the "Auspicious Eon" (*Bhadrakalpa*).

In the "Chapter on Śakra Devānām-indra," the name was established because when he was born, the minds of both humans and devas were heated with fervor; this is an explanation of the name based on its causes and conditions.
That his conduct was contrary [to worldly norms] while his principle was compliant embodies the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), not the intent of other teachings.

"In his true nature he is cool and refreshing, yet in his manifested traces he appears as if suffering from heat; this is merely because he shares in the illnesses of sentient beings. The *Baochang jingmu* states: "The *Lotus Sūtra* has been translated four times; two versions have been preserved and two have been lost."
Dharmarakṣa—this means "Dharma-Protector"—translated it in Chang'an during the Western Jin dynasty; its title is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Dharmarakṣa further expounded upon it; this is the version inherited by Daoan and Fatai.

Kumārajīva—translated as "Child Longevity" (Tóngshòu)—was a native of Kucha. On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the fifth year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty, he completed the translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang’an. By the summer of the eighth year, while translating this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Cótáng Monastery, he commissioned Sēngruì to lecture upon it; Sēngruì divided it into nine sections. At that time, there were twenty-eight chapters. Palace ladies in Chang’an requested that one chapter be withheld and kept within the palace, so that what was transmitted to Jiangdong consisted of only twenty-seven chapters.

During the Liang dynasty, there was Dharma Master Man, who lectured on the sutra one hundred times. At Changsha Commandery, he performed the practice of self-immolation by fire; he then placed this chapter before the "Chapter on Upholding" (Chih-pin), though he did so privately and it had not yet been heard of throughout the world.
The Chan Master Chen Younan placed this chapter after the "Jeweled Stupa" (Bǎotă); later, when he compared it with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they were found to correspond very closely.
"Now that the four rivers have merged and the old edition from Chang'an has been seen, we know for certain that the two masters have deeply grasped the intent of the sūtra.
Devadatta is also called Dādu; this translates as "Heavenly Fever. He led away five hundred bhikṣus to split the Saṃgha, which caused Śāriputra to become weary of him.

While [the Buddha] was fast asleep, Maudgalyāyana lifted the assembly and returned; upon waking, he made a vow to avenge this enmity. He seized a rock thirty cubits in height and fifteen cubits in width and hurled it at the Buddha. A mountain deity shielded him with his hand, but a small fragment splintered off and struck the Buddha’s foot, drawing blood.
He incited King Ajātaśatru to release a drunken elephant to trample the Buddha;
he caused the bhikṣuṇī Kuṇḍalakesā to die; and...
The ten-clawed poison-man, wishing to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, instead wounded the Buddha; this constitutes one of the five heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma).
If three such crimes are committed, it is included within the category of harming the Buddha by instructing the king and the poison-clawed man to do so together.

Because his conduct was contrary to what is appropriate, at the time of his birth, the hearts of humans and devas were inflamed with heat; he received his name from this, and thus it is called "Heavenly Heat" (Tianre), which refers to his outward manifestation (*traces*).

If one explains it according to its fundamental meaning (*essence*), it is because sentient beings suffer from afflictions that the Bodhisattva manifests heat; by sharing in their illness and conduct, he delivers and liberates them.

The purpose of this chapter is to cite ancient traditions of propagating the sutras to demonstrate that they are not erroneous in their benefit, to clarify that the efficacy of contemporary preaching and transformation is not in vain, and to exhort the present by citing the past so that [the teaching] may be widely circulated.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, up to the passage "born by transformation from a lotus before a Buddha," it clarifies that in the past, Dharmodgata mastered the sutra and Śākyamuni attained enlightenment;

second, from the passage "At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the Treasure Stupa in the lower regions" onwards, it clarifies that today Mañjuśrī masters the sutra and the dragon girl becomes a Buddha. If even those who merely receive the teaching are thus, how could the merit and benefit of proclaiming and transmitting it not be truly great!
Therefore, it is said that Devadatta received his prediction [of enlightenment] and Mañjuśrī can understand this through the power of his mind, and so forth.
This section has three parts:
first, clarifying the manner in which the teacher and disciple upheld the sūtra in the past; second, correlating the ancient and the present; and third, exhorting faith.
The first [section] on "Existence" consists of prose and verse.
The prose has four parts:
first, clarifying the timing for seeking the Dharma;
2. From "Throughout many kalpas" onwards, the text correctly explains the seeking of the Dharma;
3. From "At that time there was a rishi" onwards, it explains obtaining a Dharma teacher;
4. From "The king heard" onwards, it explains receiving the Dharma and putting it into practice.
The first [section] is as the text reads.
From "Throughout many kalpas" onwards is the second [section], which further consists of two parts:
first, the clarification of making vows; [the second part follows].
The section beginning with "In order to fulfill" has two parts, clarifying the practice.
Within the practice, there are further two:
first, clarifying the diligent performance of giving in order to fulfill *dāna*, as the text states; second... [text continues].
2. From "The people of that age" onwards, it clarifies seeking the sublime Dharma in order to fulfill the *prajñā*.
There are seven and a half verses, which versify the preceding prose.
The first two lines eulogize the first [section]:
the time for seeking the Dharma; next, from "Although he acts... onwards, the second section, one and a half lines, eulogizes the second [section]:

the actual seeking of the Dharma; next, from "At that time there was an Āsīta... onwards, the third section, one and a half lines, eulogizes the third [section]: obtaining a teacher who expounds the Dharma.
From "At that time, the king heard the words of the seer" onwards is the fourth section, consisting of two and a half lines, which praises the reception of the Dharma and its practice;
from "Later, he did not act for his own sake" onwards is the fifth section, consisting of one and a half lines, which concludes with testimony and encourages faith.
"Addressing the bhikṣus regarding the king," and so forth, is the second section, which synthesizes the ancient and the present; it further consists of two parts:
first, the formal synthesis of the ancient and the present, as in the text;
and second, from "By means of Deva," onwards, the clarification that both teacher and disciple have fulfilled their karmic rewards.
This section further contains two parts:
first, it clarifies that the disciples' causal retribution has already been fulfilled;
second, from the passage "The Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly" onwards, it clarifies that the sublime fruit of the Dharma Master shall be realized.
Among the disciples, there are again three [sections]:
first, clarifying the fulfillment of the causes;
next, from "The Thirty-two Marks" onwards, clarifying the perfection of the fruit.
Below the section "All because of Deva," the conclusion establishes the benefit derived from those who have mastered the sutras.

First, regarding "being fully endowed with the six pāramitās": the meaning of "crossing over" (pāra) is manifold, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Giving away one's person and possessions (*niśraya*) is called *dāna* (giving); preventing the sevenfold [unwholesome] actions is called *śīla* (precept); not responding to beating or reviling is called *kṣānti* (patience); persevering from beginning to end in all tasks is called *vīrya* (diligence); the four dhyānas and eight samādhis are called *dhyāna* (meditation); and resolving disputes by apportioning land is called *prajñā* (wisdom).

Furthermore, if the ten wholesome actions are condensed into six, then from non-killing up to non-lying constitutes *dāna* (generosity); non-divisive speech constitutes *śīla* (ethical discipline); non-harsh speech constitutes *kṣānti* (patience); non-frivolous speech constitutes *vīrya* (diligence); non-covetousness and non-malice constitute *dhyāna* (meditative concentration); and non-wrong view constitutes *prajñā* (wisdom).

The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, chapter ten, states: "The six pāramitās have three aspects: first, the aspect of antidotes, namely stinginess, malice, anger, indolence, distraction, and delusion, and so forth;

second, the aspect of mutual generation, meaning that one leaves home and upholds the precepts, must endure insults when encountering them, and having endured, practices diligence; having practiced diligence, one disciplines the five faculties, and once the faculties are disciplined, one realizes the dharma-realm;
third, the aspect of retribution, which consists of wealth, physical beauty, strength, longevity, peace, and eloquence."

Furthermore, another sutra states: "The retribution for giving is wealth; the retribution for morality is rebirth in the happy realms; the retribution for patience is physical beauty; the retribution for diligence is supernatural powers; the retribution for meditation is birth in the heavens; and the retribution for wisdom is the destruction of afflictions."
Examples such as these all clarify the characteristics of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) within the Tripiṭaka.

If the three factors of the giver, the recipient, and the gift are all empty, this is called *dāna* (generosity); not perceiving transgressions or observances is called *śīla* (precept); that which can endure and that which is endured being ungraspable is called *kṣānti* (patience); the non-movement of body and mind is called *vīrya* (diligence); being neither distracted nor savoring [meditative states] is called *dhyāna* (meditation); and being neither wise nor foolish is called *prajñā* (wisdom). Such categories as these constitute the characteristics of the six perfections within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

If it is said that there are ten benefits to *dāna*: it subdues the affliction of stinginess; the intention to give continues uninterruptedly; one shares assets with sentient beings; one is born into wealthy and noble families; the mind of giving manifests in every lifetime; one is cherished by the fourfold assembly; one is not timid when among the masses; one’s excellent reputation spreads far and wide; one’s hands and feet become supple; and finally, upon reaching the site of enlightenment, one always encounters virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Regarding the ten benefits of the precepts: they fulfill all-knowledge as taught by the Buddha; the wise do not disparage them; one’s vows do not regress; one dwells securely in practice; one abandons birth and death and yearns for the bliss of nirvana; one attains an unentangled mind; one attains supreme samādhi; and one does not lack the wealth of faith.

Regarding the ten benefits of patience: fire, swords, poison, and water cannot harm one; one is protected by non-humans; one’s physical form is adorned with the marks of excellence; one closes off the evil realms and is reborn in the Brahma Heaven; one is constantly at peace day and night; and the body never departs from joy and bliss.

Regarding the ten benefits of diligence: one cannot be overcome by others; one is embraced by the Buddha; one is protected by non-human beings; one does not forget the Dharma one has heard; one is able to hear what has not been heard before; one’s eloquence increases; one attains the nature of samādhi; one has little illness or affliction; one can digest whatever food is eaten; and one flourishes like the growth of an *utpala* flower.

Regarding the ten benefits of dhyāna: one dwells securely in the observance of ritual protocols and practices the sphere of loving-kindness; one is free from remorse and feverish distress; one guards the sense faculties; one attains the joy that is independent of food; one’s cultivation of dhyāna is not in vain as one leaves behind craving and desire; one is liberated from the snares of Māra and dwells securely in the realm of the Buddha; and one achieves liberation and maturation.

The perfection of wisdom has ten benefits: it does not grasp at the signs of giving; it does not rely on precepts; it does not dwell in the power of patience; it does not abandon physical and mental diligence; its meditative concentration has no fixed abode and thus demons cannot disturb it; it cannot be moved by the discourses of others; it reaches the bottom of birth and death and gives rise to supreme compassion; and it takes no pleasure in the stages of the two vehicles.
There are four matters for which one should practice dāna:
first, because it destroys stinginess and greed in those who cultivate the Path;
second, because it adorns bodhi.

Third, regarding the benefit of oneself and others: being joyful at the time of intending to give, at the time of giving, and after having given is called self-benefit; that the hunger and thirst of others are removed is called benefiting others.
Fourth, obtaining great and virtuous fruits in future lives, such as attaining great nobility and abundant wealth in future lives.
There are four reasons why one should uphold the precepts:

to cultivate wholesome dharmas for oneself and extinguish evil; to adorn bodhi with the ornament of morality and gather in sentient beings; to attain peace while sleeping and waking, to be free from regret, and to harbor no harmful intent toward sentient beings; and finally, to receive the joys of humans and devas and attain the bliss of nirvana.
There are four reasons why one should cultivate patience:

by cultivating patience, one eliminates impatience; it adorns bodhi and gathers in sentient beings; it causes oneself and others to be free from fear; and it ensures that there is no anger in future lives, that one's retinue remains unbroken, and that one does not undergo suffering, thereby attaining the bliss of humans, devas, and nirvana.
In these four matters, one must cultivate diligence:

diligence destroys indolence; it adorns bodhi and gathers in sentient beings; increasing wholesome dharmas is self-benefit, while not afflicting others is benefit for others; finally, one attains great power and realizes bodhi.
There are four matters for which one should cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):

concentration destroys the distracted mind; it adorns *bodhi* and gathers in sentient beings; tranquility of body and mind is self-benefit, while not afflicting sentient beings is benefit for others; and finally, one receives a pure body and peacefully attains *nirvāṇa*.
There are four matters for which one should cultivate *prajñā*:

wisdom destroys ignorance; it adorns *bodhi* and gathers in sentient beings. Wisdom that finds joy within itself is self-benefit; its ability to teach sentient beings is the benefit of others; and its power to destroy afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) constitutes its great fruit.
Such precedents illustrate the characteristics of the six perfections as explained in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*).

The first fascicle of the *Candragarbha-sūtra* states: "If sentient beings seek bodhi solely by relying on recitation and chanting, such persons are attached to the mundane; since they have not even tamed their own afflictions, how could they possibly tame others?"

This person, being attached to jealousy, fame, profit, wealth, and honor, with a haughty mind considering themselves right while disparaging and slandering others, cannot even attain the roots of goodness of the desire realm, much less those of the form and formless realms.
How much less so the bodhi of the two vehicles,
and how much less so the unsurpassed bodhi?
It is like a spark from a firefly that cannot dry up the ocean, breath from the mouth that cannot move a mountain, or a lotus fiber that cannot weigh a peak.
Why is this? The conventional cannot fulfill bodhi.
What is the ultimate truth?

This refers to performing all meritorious deeds—whether cultivating the body, cultivating the mind, or cultivating wisdom—and practicing through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), whereby one swiftly fulfills the six *pāramitās*:

If, whether walking or sitting, one abandons thoughts of objective referents (*ālambana*), this is *dāna* (generosity). If one abandons objective referents and does not transgress, this is *śīla* (ethical discipline). If no afflictions arise regarding sensory objects, this is *kṣānti* (patience). If one does not abandon detachment, this is *vīrya* (diligence). If one is not heedless amidst activities, this is *dhyāna* (meditative concentration). If one realizes that the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is non-arising, this is *prajñā* (wisdom).

Furthermore, relinquishing the aggregates (*skandha*) is *dāna*; not conceptualizing or dwelling upon the aggregates is *śīla*; being without the notion of a self within the aggregates is *kṣānti*; giving rise to the perception of enmity toward the aggregates is *vīrya*; not being inflamed by the aggregates is *dhyāna*; and ultimately abandoning the aggregates is *prajñā*.

Renouncing the elements is *dāna*; not agitating or turbidizing the elements is *śīla*; relinquishing the causal conditions within the elements is *kṣānti*; repeatedly relinquishing within the elements is *vīrya*; non-arising within the elements is *dhyāna*; and regarding the elements as being like illusions is *prajñā*.
Such as these are called the profound essential teachings on the skillful means of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which are able to fulfill the six *pāramitās*.
Whether practiced for oneself or for others, all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time cultivate these dharmas to achieve *bodhi*; therefore, they are not mundane.
This Dharma can pacify the suffering of the path of afflictions and the path of sentient beings, and establish them upon the path to Bodhi.
Only in the seventh stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is it clearly elucidated that, in every thought-moment, one is endowed with the ten pāramitās and cultivates all Buddha-dharmas.

To share roots of goodness for seeking the Buddha-way with all sentient beings is *dāna*; to be able to extinguish the heat of all afflictions is *śīla*; to cause no harm to any sentient being is *kṣānti*; to seek the good without weariness is *vīrya*; to have a mind that does not scatter while cultivating the Way, constantly directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), is *dhyāna*; to endure the gate of the non-arising of all phenomena is *prajñā*; to be able to give rise to immeasurable gates of wisdom is *upāya*; to seek ever-superior wisdom is *praṇidhāna*; that which cannot be obstructed by Māra or heterodoxies is *bala*; and to explain the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are is *jñāna*. Because these ten *pāramitās* are complete, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and all factors conducive to enlightenment are fully perfected in every thought-moment; all stages (*bhūmi*) are fully perfected in every thought-moment, because this stage is preeminent.
Such examples illustrate the characteristics of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Next, following the section on the "Thirty-two Marks" (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), the perfection of the fruit is elucidated.

Regarding the "Thirty-two Marks": the soles of the feet are level like the bottom of a casket; the insteps are prominent like the shell of a tortoise. These two marks together result from the cultivation of firm and steadfast giving (*dāna*).
The single mark of the thousand-spoked wheel is cultivated through one practice: providing comfort to those who are terrified.
Three marks—the long heels, the long fingers and toes, and the straight, rounded body—are cultivated together through one practice: the precept of refraining from taking life.
Seven marks—the seven parts of the body being full, the shoulders, the neck, the arms, and the feet—are cultivated through one practice: constantly acting as a donor.
The webbed hands and feet and their softness constitute two marks resulting from one practice, namely, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The straight heels, the inconspicuous ankles, and the hair curling to the right constitute three marks resulting from one practice: constantly benefiting sentient beings with wholesome dharmas.
The deer-like calves constitute one mark resulting from one practice: teaching people through scriptures without parsimony.
The mark of skin that receives no dust or grime is cultivated through one practice: answering questions exactly as they are asked.
The golden-hued complexion is cultivated through one practice: practicing patience and giving fine garments.
The mark of the horse-like sheath of the private parts is cultivated through one practice: reconciling disputes and litigation.
The mark of the Brahma-body being perfectly round and the mark of the hands reaching the knees are cultivated together; through these, one teaches with a mind of loving-kindness and so forth.
The marks of the rounded shoulders, the halo around the neck, and the lion-like chest are cultivated together as three aspects; through these, one constantly causes the merit of giving to increase.
The mark of the *svastika* on the palms is cultivated as one; through this, one does not afflict sentient beings.
The deep blue eyes and eyelashes like those of a bull-king: these two marks are cultivated together through not looking upon sentient beings with anger or lust.
The cranial protuberance and the dark blue hair: these two marks are cultivated together so that all merits precede one.
A single hair growing from each pore and the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows: these two marks are cultivated together through refraining from false speech.
Forty teeth, white and even—these two marks are cultivated together through refraining from double-tongued speech;
a broad and long tongue and a Brahma-like voice—these two marks are cultivated together through refraining from harsh speech;
and lion-like jaws—one mark is cultivated through refraining from frivolous speech.
The fourth tooth is cultivated to abandon wrong livelihood. The merit of all sentient beings combined is equal to that of a single hair of the Buddha;

the merit of all the Buddha’s hairs is equal to that of one secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*); all the secondary marks are equal to one primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*); all the primary marks are equal to the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) and the crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*); and it takes hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of such merits for the white tuft and the crown-protrusion to produce the Brahma-voice.

Although the causes for each of the thirty-two marks are distinct, when discussing their true cause, it is the observance of precepts and diligence; for if one lacks precepts despite being diligent, one cannot even attain the bodies of humans or devas, let alone the other marks.
This is the fundamental basis for the characteristics of the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

Emptiness and non-arising are the fundamental basis for the characteristics of the Shared Teaching; the Knowledge of the Modes of the Path is the fundamental basis for the characteristics of the Distinct Teaching; and the True Reality is the fundamental basis for the characteristics of the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the "eighty secondary marks" (*anuvyañjana*): the twenty fingers and toes, both on the palms and soles; eight places that are level and full;
six places—the ankles, knees, and thighs—that are excellent; six places—the shoulders, elbows, and wrists—that are full; three places—the two hip-bones and the center of the navel—that are excellent;

two places—the hips and buttocks—where the private parts are concealed as in a horse; two places—the upper arms and the waist—that are even; six places—the sides, armpits, and breasts; four places—the abdomen, chest, back, and neck; the upper and lower teeth, the upper and lower lips and palate, the two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyes, the two eyebrows, the two nostrils, the forehead, the two hair-tufts, the two ears, and the roundness of the head. If one analyzes the meaning of these four types of marks, they may be understood by analogy with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Announcing to the fourfold assembly," and so forth, is the second section, clarifying that the Master’s wondrous fruition shall be attained.
Within this section on the Master, there are three parts;
first, clarifying the attainment of the primary fruition.

The *Pundarīka Sūtra* states: "Devadatta shall become a Buddha named T'i-ho-lo-ye (Devānām-indra); in the Han language, this means 'Heavenly King. His land shall be named T'i-ho-yueh; in the Han language, this means 'Heaven and Earth.'"
"From 'At that time, the World-Honored Tathāgata King of Heaven remained in the world for twenty [years]' onwards is the second section, clarifying the transformation and deliverance.
From 'At that time, the World-Honored Tathāgata King of Heaven entered parinirvāṇa' onwards is the third section, clarifying the benefits after his passing."
From "The Buddha told the bhikṣus" onwards is the third section, the exhortation to practice, as per the text.

Regarding "birth by transformation from a lotus," the *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sūtra) states: "Those born from a lotus are not the 'transformation-born' among the four modes of birth—namely, womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. It is called "transformation" though it is not [the same as] transformation; in reality, it is not like the transformation-born among the four modes of birth.

The *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* states, "Birth by transformation from a lotus serves as one's parents," while the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-vyūha-dhyāna-sūtra* states, "Those who dwell for a long time upon the lotus pedestal are said to be 'womb-born,' yet they are not truly born from a womb; likewise, those born from a lotus are also termed 'moisture-born' or 'egg-born,' yet they are neither moisture-born nor egg-born," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "At that time, from below," the second section clarifies how Mañjuśrī benefits others through his mastery of this sutra today; this is further divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies Mañjuśrī’s mastery of the sutra;
second, from the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī said, 'I [was] in the midst of the ocean,'" it clarifies the benefits.
The first group further consists of five:
first, the request for withdrawal by Prajñākūṭa.
The *Puṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "From the Buddha’s realm below, there was a bodhisattva named Prajñākūṭa; in the Han language, this means 'Accumulation of Wisdom' (*Zhìjī*)."
2. From "Śākyamuni" onwards, it clarifies that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni stops [the assembly] to demonstrate the proof of the benefits derived from the universal circulation of the sutra.
Jñatikūṭa stated that he had emerged for the purpose of witnessing the sutra; now that his exhortation for its circulation is complete, he requests to return.

Regarding the cessation of Śākyamuni: although the events of the Trace Gate (Jikimon) have concluded, the Essential Gate (Honmon) has not yet been revealed; therefore, he entrusts [the stupa] to Mañjuśrī to preserve it for Prabhūtaratna. The Buddha’s secret intention is not something that bodhisattvas can know.
From "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards is the third section: Mañjuśrī’s arrival.
Fourth, from "The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa... onwards, Jñānakūṭa asks how many beings have been transformed.
5. From "Mañjuśrī said" onwards, Mañjuśrī’s response is not something proclaimed by the mouth.
This fifth section further divides into seven parts;
the first is the response that the benefits are exceedingly great.
"From 'The words spoken have not yet... below is the second section, the assembly of those who have received benefit as witnesses.
"From 'These various bodhisattvas... below is the third section, all of whom were transformed by Mañjuśrī.
"Original Śrāvakas," below: Fourth, regarding original śrāvakas, they previously received the provisional teachings and dwelt in the path of the two vehicles.
The *Puṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "As for the lotuses that emerge from the pond, those whose original aspiration was for bodhicitta have their flowers speak of Mahāyāna matters while in mid-air;
those whose original aspiration was for the śrāvaka mind have their flowers speak only of severing birth and death while in mid-air."
From "From now on, all shall practice" onwards is the fifth section: having now heard the teaching of reality, they all abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
From "Mañjuśrī addressed Zhijizhang" onwards is the sixth section: Mañjuśrī’s summary of the benefits.
From "At that time" onwards, there are seven verses of accumulated stanzas in praise.
From "Mañjuśrī said: 'In the midst of the ocean... onwards is the second section, clarifying the benefits.

The text consists of nine sections: first, Mañjuśrī’s self-narration; second, the questioning by Jñānakūṭa; third, the response; fourth, Jñānakūṭa’s adherence to the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna) as a basis for doubt; fifth, the Dragon Girl’s clarification through the Perfect Teaching to resolve that doubt; sixth, Śāriputra’s challenge based on the provisional authority of the Tripiṭaka; seventh, the Dragon Girl’s removal of doubt through the One Reality; eighth, the assembly’s attainment of benefit upon hearing and seeing; ninth, the silent faith and submission of Jñānakūṭa and Śāriputra.
Fifth, the Dragon Girl’s Elucidation of Doubts through Perfect Clarity:
First, the Sūtra describes her appearance and her expression of reverence.
Next, there are three and a half verses, which are divided into three parts:
The first half-verse clarifies that by upholding this sutra one attains liberation;
the next two verses clarify the accomplishment of the two bodies;
and the final verse cites the Buddha as testimony.

Regarding "sin and merit," these are transmitted through the seven stages of expedient means; now, this verse profoundly penetrates the absence of both sin and merit to enter the single true reality, which is termed "profound penetration."
"The ten directions" refers to the ten dharma-realms; because they are all illuminated by true wisdom, it is called "pervasive illumination.

Regarding "possessing the thirty-two marks," this means that by profoundly attaining the principle of the Dharma-body, one is already endowed with the primary and secondary marks. As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

"If one wishes to attain all dharmas, one should study Prajñā, just as one obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel. In contrast, the two vehicles merely attain emptiness, and emptiness possesses no marks or signs, and so forth.
Sixth, Śāriputra raises further objections: first, he generally challenges the credibility [of the teaching], and subsequently, he explains five obstacles.
Seventh, the dragon girl provides manifest proof; this section has two parts:
first, she offers a pearl to symbolize her attainment of perfect understanding.

The perfect sphere symbolizes the cultivation and attainment of the perfect cause; offering it to the Buddha signifies bringing forth the fruit through that cause. That the Buddha accepts it swiftly indicates the rapid attainment of the fruit. This is precisely what is meant by attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment upon the site of enlightenment, proving it to be no empty claim.
Second, it correctly demonstrates the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit.
The *Tāijīng* (Womb Sūtra) states: "The daughters of Māra, Brahmā, and Śakra do not discard their bodies nor receive new bodies; all attain Buddhahood within their current physical forms."

The verse says: "The nature of phenomena is like a great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong. Whether ordinary person or sage, all are equal without high or low. It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements; to realize this is as easy as turning over one's palm."
Eighth, from "At that time, in this Sahā world" onwards, it clarifies what the assembly saw and heard; this section further has two parts:
first, clarifying what was seen and heard;
second, the joy of humans and devas, and how both benefited one another.

In the southern lands, where conditions were ripe, it was appropriate to manifest the Way through the eight phases of enlightenment; in this land, however, where conditions were thin, he merely used a dragon girl for instruction—this is the power of skillful means.
It is the attainment of the single body as all bodies, the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Form Body.
The "Chapter on Upholding" (Shichi-pin) is so named because twenty thousand bodhisattvas received the command to propagate the sutra;
it is called the "Chapter on Exhorting to Uphold" (Quanchi-pin) because they were again exhorted to propagate the sutra by eighty quadrillion nayutas.
Question:
Why is that? Answer:

The "twenty thousand" refers to the specific number of those individually commanded at the beginning of the "Dharma-Teacher Chapter"; therefore, they were commissioned to receive and uphold [the teaching]. As for the "eighty million nayutas" and so forth mentioned previously, there was no separate command for them; that was merely a general solicitation.

Now, the Buddha gazes with his Buddha-eye and causes them to make a vow to propagate this sutra in this land; because the verification of propagating the sutra is profound and the Buddha’s intention is earnest, they propagate it upon receiving this exhortation—thus there are two intentions.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of receiving and maintaining [the precepts]; second, the explanation of exhorting others to maintain them.
The first part further consists of three sections:

First, twenty thousand bodhisattvas received the command to uphold this sutra in this land; second, five hundred and eighty thousand śrāvakas vowed to circulate it in other lands; third, the bhikṣuṇīs requested a prediction [of their future attainment].
Question:
These śrāvakas have already become mahāsattvas; for what reason are they unable to propagate this sūtra in this land?
Answer:

This is intended to guide beginner bodhisattvas who have only recently begun their practice and are unable to endure the hardships of the degenerate age while seeking to master the sutras; furthermore, it seeks to open up the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices.
The second section, "Exhortation to Uphold," consists of both prose and verse.
The prose section consists of five parts:

first, the Buddha’s gaze; second, the Bodhisattva’s request; third, the Buddha’s silence; fourth, the Bodhisattva’s understanding of his intention; and fifth, the making of vows to propagate the sutra.

As for the Buddha’s silent exhortation through his gaze rather than by speaking: although he has not specifically commanded them above, he has already clearly cited the profound depth of the merit of upholding this sutra as proof; furthermore, the Many Treasures Buddha and his emanations have come from afar to urge them on. Since the earnestness of this matter and its significance are sufficient, those who wish to respond to the summons should immediately make their vows without the need for further words. Moreover, he does not praise them aloud out of consideration for the aspirations of the śrāvakas from other regions.
The verses consist of twenty lines requesting the protection and upholding of the sutra; they are not further subdivided, as they can be understood by following the text.
The first seventeen lines concern wearing the robe of patience to propagate the sutra;
the next two lines concern entering the chamber to propagate the sutra.
Next, the third section, one paragraph, concerns sitting upon a seat to propagate the sutras;
next, the fourth section, one paragraph, is a general conclusion requesting empowerment.
The *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle six, states: "Āraṇya is translated here as 'place of no affairs'; dhūta is translated here as 'shaking off'."

The *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, chapter six, states: "When a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) sees a king, a prince, a brāhmaṇa, or any other person approaching, the bhikṣu should say, 'Welcome! Please come and sit here. If they sit down, he should sit with them; if they do not sit, he should likewise not sit. He should then preach the Dharma for their sake so that they may be filled with joy."

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the final age of evil, there will be bhikṣus who do not conform to the proper form; though they recite the precepts, they live merely for their livelihood and take no pleasure in practicing them. This applies to all five elements of the Dharma-body, and likewise to all other dharmas of the Path. It is like a person with a runny nose describing sandalwood: though he speaks of it, he has no fragrance himself and cannot even smell it. Devas, humans, nāgas, and kumbhāṇḍas will never make offerings to one who lacks the precepts. The same applies to the remaining four elements. There is no way to bring forth the wondrous Dharma; it must necessarily arise from pure precepts, and the same holds true for the other four."

If one encounters the most grievous illness of impending death, oppressed by pain and suffering with no hope of recovery, yet never abandons the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, then even though all intense sufferings seize the heart, that person, through their own realization of this Dharma, shall know that all phenomena are empty.
Regarding the "Armor of Forbearance," the fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* states: "The bhikṣu Kālakāya addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Śāriputra reviled me and spoke ill of me.'"
The Buddha quickly called to Śāriputra,
"Did you truly speak in such a way?
Śāriputra replied:
"One whose mind is unsettled may speak insults, but my mind is already settled; why should I speak insults?

Like a bull with broken horns that does not gore or harass people, like a castrated youth who, out of shame, does not disturb others, my mind is like earth, water, fire, and wind—it accepts the pure and the impure, excrement and urine, mucus and saliva, yet it does not revile them. My mind is like a broom, sweeping away both the pure and the impure. Furthermore, it is like a broken vessel filled with fat placed in the sun, from which drops constantly leak; observing that my own nine orifices are constantly leaking impurity, how could I speak insults to another?"
"Furthermore, it is like having a dead snake, a dog, or the like tied around the neck of a pure youth; he feels shame and self-reproach, and does not revile or speak ill of others.
The Buddha asked:
"How do you regard such evil people?"
He replied:
"There are five types of persons:

First, one whose body is virtuous but whose speech and mind are not. One should contemplate only their virtue and not their non-virtue; just as a monk who wears rag-robes sees a heap of refuse containing tattered cloth, grasping the left side while stretching out the right, he cuts away the impure and takes the pure. He contemplates using the purity of that person's body to regulate his own body, and discarding [the faults of] their speech and mind to admonish his own speech and mind."

Furthermore, if one’s verbal conduct is pure while one’s bodily and mental conduct are impure, one should attend to the purity of the mouth and abandon the body and mind; this is like a person suffering from heat and thirst who encounters a large grassy pond, parts the grass, scoops up water, and cools their body and quenches their thirst.

Furthermore, when the mind is pure while the body and speech are impure, one should attend to the mind and disregard the body and speech. It is like being parched with thirst on a journey where there is but a small amount of water in a cow’s footprint; if I were to scoop it up with my hands, the water would become turbid. Therefore, I should kneel on both knees, rest my mouth upon my two hands, and draw the water in by suction to eliminate the heat and thirst.

Furthermore, regarding those whose three karmas are entirely impure: although there may be nothing that can be done for them, one should contemplate their plight with deep compassion. Just as one would see a sick person on the road and settle them into a comfortable position, one should reflect upon these impurities so that they may encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who can treat their three karmas, ensuring they do not fall into the three miserable realms.

Furthermore, all three types are pure; one should constantly keep such people in mind as a model for self-instruction, maintaining equality in mindfulness and equality in aspiration. Just as a cool pond abounding with various flowers and grasses allows those suffering from heat and thirst to enter it for relief and refreshment, one should constantly keep the objective realm in mind to eliminate one's own evils.

The *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle eight, states: 'The thought of being reviled is a single word; the rest are all mere sounds. What is the use of being called out to all day long? "
Furthermore, what is disparaging speech in this region may be laudatory speech in another; if I dwell upon these disparaging words, I shall find no place for happiness.
Moreover, observe that these characters used for abuse, if their order were reversed, would instead constitute praise.
Furthermore, abuse is but a small portion of one element (dhātu), a small portion of one sense-base (āyatana), and a small portion of one aggregate (skandha); it is a little that is abused, not much.
Moreover, who is it that accomplishes abuse? It is the abuser who accomplishes it; since it is accomplished by him, what does it matter to me?

Furthermore, "abuse" consists of two characters; a single character does not constitute abuse, but it is with two characters that abuse is formed. Yet there is no time when both characters are uttered simultaneously; if one utters the latter character, the former character has already ceased.
Furthermore, both the one who reviles and the one who is reviled perish simultaneously in a single kṣaṇa;
